name: Hawwa
line: Adam's wife, created from the same soul, who lived with him in the Garden and came down with him to earth.
story: Allah created Adam's mate from him so he might find rest in her. They lived in the Garden and were told not to approach one tree. Shaytan whispered to both, they ate, and both turned to Allah together: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. They were sent down to earth, forgiven, and every human descends from them.
lesson: In the Quran the first mistake and the first repentance were shared, not blamed on the woman.
when: At the beginning of humankind (no known date)
note: The Quran calls her only 'your wife'; the name Hawwa comes from the hadith and tradition.

name: Habil
line: The son of Adam whose offering was accepted, and who refused to raise his hand against his brother.
story: Two sons of Adam each made an offering. Allah accepted Habil's and not his brother's, who then threatened to kill him. Habil answered: Allah accepts only from the God-fearing, and if you raise your hand to kill me, I will not raise mine to kill you. His brother killed him, the first murder on earth.
lesson: Whoever kills one soul unjustly, it is as if he killed all of humanity (5:32).
when: In the first generation of humankind (no known date)
note: The Quran says only 'the two sons of Adam'; the names Habil and Qabil come from the commentators.

name: Azar
line: Ibrahim's father, an idol-maker whom his son called to Allah with gentle words.
story: Ibrahim asked his father: why worship what neither hears nor sees? He spoke softly, calling him 'my dear father'. Azar threatened to stone him and drove him away. Ibrahim answered with peace and prayed for his forgiveness, until it became clear to him that his father was an enemy of Allah, and he stopped.
lesson: Ibrahim shows how to call a parent to truth: with gentleness, patience and respect.
when: In the time of Ibrahim (traditional, around 2000 BCE)
note: Named only in 6:74. Some scholars say Azar was a title or the name of an idol, or that he was Ibrahim's uncle, since Genesis calls the father Terah; most take the Quran's wording plainly.

name: Sarah
line: Ibrahim's wife, who laughed when angels told her she would bear Ishaq in old age.
story: Sarah migrated with Ibrahim and stayed with him through years without a child. When angel guests came, she was standing by and laughed at the news of a son, and of Yaqub after him. She struck her face: shall I bear a child, an old woman, with my husband an old man? The angels said: do you wonder at the decree of Allah?
legacy: Through her son Ishaq came Yaqub and the prophets of Bani Israil.
when: In the time of Ibrahim (traditional, around 1950 BCE)
note: The Quran calls her 'his wife'; she is named in hadith.

name: The Daughters of Lut
line: Lut's daughters, saved with him from the overturned towns while his wife was left behind.
story: When his people surrounded his guests, Lut pointed to his daughters and said: these are my daughters, they are purer for you, meaning lawful marriage. The angels told him to leave by night with his family. In the whole town Allah found only one household of believers, and they were brought out safe.
lesson: A single believing household can be the only one saved in a whole town.
note: Many commentators say 'my daughters' means the women of his nation, since a prophet is like a father to his people. Their names in some books come from Isra'iliyyat.

name: The Wife of Ayyub
line: Ayyub's wife, who stayed by him through years of illness and loss.
story: When Ayyub lost his health, wealth and children, she alone, the commentators say, remained to care for him. Ayyub once swore in anger to strike her. When Allah healed him, He gave him an easy way to keep the oath without harming her: take a bundle of grass and strike with it. He also restored his family to him, and doubled.
lesson: Faithfulness in hard years is honoured by Allah, and so is mercy towards a spouse.
when: In the time of Ayyub (date unknown)
note: The Quran alludes to her only through the oath in 38:44. Her name, often given as Rahmah, and her story come from the commentators.

name: The Brothers of Yusuf
line: Yusuf's ten older brothers who threw him in a well and, years later, begged his forgiveness in Egypt.
story: Jealous of their father's love, they dropped Yusuf into a well and brought Yaqub a shirt with false blood. Decades later famine drove them to Egypt, where the minister they bowed to was Yusuf himself. He said: no blame on you today. They asked their father to pray for them, and he did.
lesson: Envy can tear a family apart; forgiveness can put it back together.
when: In the time of Yaqub and Yusuf
note: Some scholars counted them among 'the tribes' (al-asbat) given revelation; most say the asbat are their descendants and that the brothers were not prophets.

name: The Eldest Brother
line: The brother who refused to leave Egypt without Binyamin, ashamed to face his father.
story: When Binyamin was held in Egypt, the brothers despaired and spoke privately. The eldest reminded them of their oath to Yaqub and of how they had failed him over Yusuf. He said: I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah judges for me. He sent the others home to tell the truth.
lesson: Keeping a promise sometimes means staying behind alone.
note: The commentators name him Rubil (Reuben) or Yahudha (Judah). Some say he was also the brother in 12:10 who said 'do not kill Yusuf'.

name: Binyamin
line: Yusuf's younger full brother, whom Yusuf kept with him in Egypt by a plan from Allah.
story: Yaqub loved Yusuf and his brother most, which stirred the others' jealousy. Years later Yusuf asked for this brother to be brought to Egypt and quietly told him who he was. He placed the king's cup in his bag so that, under the law, he could keep him. That led to the family's reunion.
lesson: Allah's plans can look like hardship until the end of the story.
note: The Quran calls him 'his brother'; the name Binyamin comes from the commentators and the Torah.

name: The Aziz of Egypt
line: The Egyptian official who bought the boy Yusuf and told his wife: make his stay honourable.
story: He bought Yusuf from travellers for a few coins and hoped to adopt him. When his wife accused Yusuf, a witness showed from the torn shirt that Yusuf was innocent, and the Aziz told her to seek forgiveness. Even so, Yusuf was later put in prison to quiet the talk.
note: 'Al-Aziz' is a title, roughly 'the mighty one' or chief minister. The commentators name him Qitfir or Itfir; Genesis calls Yusuf's master Potiphar.

name: The Wife of the Aziz
line: The Aziz's wife who tried to seduce Yusuf, then, years later, confessed his innocence before the king.
story: She locked the doors and called Yusuf to herself; he said: I seek refuge in Allah. Caught at the door, she accused him, but his shirt was torn from behind. When women mocked her, she showed them Yusuf and they cut their hands in amazement. Years later she admitted: it was I who sought to seduce him.
lesson: Truth comes out in the end, and admitting a wrong is a kind of honour.
note: The name Zulaykha (or Ra'il) comes from the commentators, not the Quran. The story that she later married Yusuf is from later lore and has no sound basis.

name: The Witness from Her Family
line: A member of the Aziz's wife's own family who proved Yusuf innocent by the torn shirt.
story: When Yusuf and the woman both stood accused at the door, a witness from her family said: if his shirt is torn from the front, she is truthful; if from the back, she has lied. The shirt was torn from the back. Her own relative's reasoning cleared Yusuf.
lesson: Fair judgement looks at evidence, even when it goes against your own family.
note: Commentators differ: some say he was a baby in the cradle who spoke, citing a weak narration; others, including Ibn Abbas in one report, say he was a wise man of her household.

name: The Women of the City
line: Noblewomen of Egypt who gossiped about the Aziz's wife, then cut their hands at the sight of Yusuf.
story: They whispered that the Aziz's wife was chasing her servant. She invited them to a banquet, handed each a knife, and called Yusuf out. Struck by him, they cut their hands and said: this is no man, this is a noble angel. Later, questioned by the king, they testified: we know nothing bad about him.
lesson: Those quick to judge others often fail the same test.

name: Yusuf's Fellow Prisoners
line: Two young men in prison with Yusuf whose dreams he interpreted, after first calling them to Allah.
story: One dreamed he was pressing wine, the other that birds were eating bread from his head. Before explaining, Yusuf told them about the One God: O my two companions of prison, are many lords better, or Allah, the One? One would serve wine to his master; the other would be crucified. The freed man forgot Yusuf for years, then remembered at the king's dream.
lesson: Yusuf used every moment, even in prison, to speak about Allah.
note: The commentators say one was the king's cupbearer and the other his baker.

name: The King of Egypt
line: The ruler whose dream of seven fat and seven thin cows brought Yusuf out of prison to power.
story: No one at court could explain his dream until the freed prisoner remembered Yusuf. Yusuf read it: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine. Before leaving prison he asked the king to clear his name. Then the king said: bring him, I will take him for myself, and placed him over the storehouses of the land.
lesson: A wise ruler listens to the right person, even one found in prison.
note: The Quran calls him 'the king' (al-malik), not Firaun as in Musa's story. Many link this to the Hyksos rulers of Egypt. The commentators name him al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid.

name: The Mother of Musa
line: The mother inspired by Allah to place her baby in the river, and promised he would return to her.
story: Firaun was killing the newborn sons of Bani Israil. Allah inspired her: nurse him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river and do not grieve; We will return him to you and make him a messenger. Her heart became empty with worry, but Allah strengthened her. Within days she was nursing him again, paid by Firaun's own house.
lesson: Letting go in trust of Allah is sometimes the only way to keep what you love.
note: The Quran does not name her. The commentators call her Yukabid (Jochebed).

name: The Sister of Musa
line: The girl who followed baby Musa along the river and led Firaun's household back to her own mother.
story: Her mother told her: follow him. She watched from a distance while Firaun's household drew him out, unnoticed. The baby refused every wet nurse. Then she stepped forward: shall I show you a family who will care for him? So Musa was returned to his mother, and her eyes were cooled.
lesson: A quick, brave word from a child can change history.
note: The commentators name her Maryam or Kulthum. She is not Maryam the mother of Isa, whose family is called 'sister of Harun' in 19:28 in another sense.

name: Asiya
line: Firaun's wife, who raised Musa and chose a house with Allah in Paradise over a palace on earth.
story: When the baby was drawn from the river, she said: a comfort of the eye for me and for you, do not kill him. She raised Musa in the palace. Later she believed, and the Quran gives her as an example for all believers: she prayed, my Lord, build for me a house near You in Paradise, and save me from Firaun and his deeds.
legacy: The Prophet ﷺ named her among the women who reached perfection.
lesson: Faith can live in the house of the worst tyrant.
when: In the time of Musa (traditional, around 1300 BCE)
note: The Quran calls her 'the wife of Firaun'; the name Asiya bint Muzahim is from hadith. That she was tortured to death for her faith is reported by the commentators.

name: The Man of Musa's People
line: The Israelite whose fight with an Egyptian led to Musa's accidental killing and flight from Egypt.
story: Musa entered the city and found two men fighting, one of his people and one of his enemy. The Israelite called for help, and Musa struck the Egyptian, who died. Musa repented at once. The next day the same man was fighting again and cried out for help; Musa told him he was clearly a troublemaker, and the secret came out.
lesson: Musa called his own blow the work of Shaytan and asked forgiveness straight away.

name: The Man Who Warned Musa
line: A man who ran from the far end of the city to warn Musa of a plot to kill him.
story: After the killing became known, Firaun's chiefs met to decide Musa's death. A man came running from the farthest part of the city: O Musa, the chiefs are conferring to kill you, so leave; I am a sincere adviser to you. Musa left at once, fearful and watchful, praying to be saved from the wrongdoing people.
lesson: One honest warning, given at the right time, can save a prophet.
when: Just before Musa fled to Madyan
note: Some commentators say he was the same believer of Firaun's family who spoke out in Surah Ghafir.

name: The Old Man of Madyan
line: The aged father of two daughters, who sheltered the fleeing Musa and married him to one of them.
story: His daughters could not water their flock until the shepherds left, for their father was a very old man. Musa watered it for them, and the father sent for him. Hearing his story, he said: do not fear, you have escaped the wrongdoing people. He offered Musa a daughter in marriage for eight or ten years of work.
lesson: Recognising good character in a stranger, and acting on it, is wisdom.
note: Many say he was the prophet Shuayb. Others, including Ibn Kathir's discussion, doubt it because of the long gap between Shuayb's people and Musa, and suggest a relative of Shuayb or a righteous man called Yathrun (Jethro).

name: Safura
line: The modest young woman of Madyan who said of Musa: hire him, he is strong and trustworthy.
story: She and her sister held back their flock at the well of Madyan until Musa watered it for them. Sent to fetch him, she came walking with shyness. She told her father: hire him, the best you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy. She became Musa's wife and travelled with him back towards Egypt.
lesson: Strength and trustworthiness together are the qualities to look for.
note: The Quran does not name her; Safura (Zipporah) comes from the commentators and the Torah. Which sister Musa married is not stated in the Quran.

name: The Sister of Safura
line: The second daughter at the well of Madyan, who waited with her sister until Musa helped them.
story: Two women stood apart from the crowd at the well, holding back their animals. Asked why, they said: we cannot water until the shepherds leave, and our father is a very old man. Their modesty and their father's age moved Musa to help. It was the start of his new life in Madyan.
lesson: Musa helped two strangers when he himself was homeless and hungry.
note: Some commentators call her Layya or Sharfa; the names are from the commentators.

name: The Believer of Firaun's Family
line: A man of Firaun's own family who hid his faith, then spoke out to defend Musa before the court.
story: When Firaun proposed killing Musa, this man stood up: will you kill a man for saying my Lord is Allah? He warned them of the fate of Nuh's people, Ad and Thamud, and of the Day of Calling. He entrusted his affair to Allah, and Allah protected him from their evil plans.
lesson: One voice of truth at the court of power is remembered in the Quran forever.
note: The Quran does not name him; the commentators give names such as Hizqil or Sam'an. Some say he was Firaun's cousin.

name: The Magicians of Firaun
line: Egypt's best sorcerers, brought to defeat Musa, who instead fell down in prostration and believed.
story: They came on the day of the festival hoping for a reward. Their ropes and staffs seemed to slither, but Musa's staff swallowed what they had faked. They knew it was no magic and fell prostrate: we believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa. Firaun threatened to cut off their hands and feet and crucify them. They answered: decide what you will.
lesson: Faith can change a person completely in a single moment.
note: Whether Firaun carried out his threat is not stated in the Quran; Ibn Abbas is reported to have said they began the day as magicians and ended it as martyrs.

name: Yusha ibn Nun
line: Musa's young companion on the journey to al-Khidr, who later led Bani Israil into the holy land.
story: He carried the fish on Musa's journey to meet al-Khidr, and forgot to mention when it slipped into the sea, a sign of the meeting place. The commentators also say he was one of the two God-fearing men who urged the people to enter the holy land. After the forty years of wandering he led them in.
legacy: Many scholars count him as a prophet; he is the Joshua of the Bible.
when: In the time of Musa and after
note: The Quran calls him 'his servant / young man'; he is named Yusha ibn Nun in the hadith. His role in 5:23 is from the commentators.

name: Kalib ibn Yufanna
role: One of the two who feared
line: One of two God-fearing men who told Bani Israil to enter the holy land and trust Allah.
story: Musa told his people to enter the land Allah had written for them. They refused, fearing a mighty people there. Two men who feared Allah said: enter on them through the gate, and when you enter you will prevail; rely on Allah if you are believers. The people still refused, and wandered forty years.
lesson: Courage with trust in Allah is rarer than fear, and Allah praised it.
note: The Quran says 'two men'; the commentators identify them as Yusha ibn Nun and Kalib (Caleb).

name: Al-Khidr
line: A servant of Allah given knowledge from Him, whom Musa travelled to learn from.
story: Musa found him where the two seas meet and asked to follow him. Al-Khidr made a hole in a boat, killed a boy and rebuilt a falling wall for nothing. Musa could not keep silent. At the end al-Khidr explained: the boat was saved from a tyrant, the parents from a cruel son, and two orphans' treasure kept safe. I did not do it of my own accord.
lesson: Behind what looks like harm, Allah's wisdom may be working.
note: The Quran calls him 'a servant of Ours'; the name al-Khidr is from the hadith. Scholars differ on whether he was a prophet (the stronger view for many) or a righteous saint, and on whether he is still alive. The meeting place is unknown; Sinai's southern tip is one suggestion.

name: Talut
line: The king Allah chose for Bani Israil for his knowledge and strength, though he had no wealth.
story: Bani Israil asked a prophet for a king to fight under. When Allah chose Talut they objected that he was not rich. Their prophet said Allah gave him knowledge and stature, and the Ark returned, carried by angels, as a sign. Talut tested his army at a river; only a few passed. With them, and young Dawud, he defeated Jalut.
lesson: Allah gives leadership to whom He wills, and it is knowledge and strength that count, not money.
note: Usually identified with the biblical Saul. The prophet who appointed him is named Shamwil (Samuel) by the commentators.

name: Luqman
line: A wise man given wisdom by Allah, whose advice to his son fills a surah of the Quran.
story: Allah gave Luqman wisdom: be grateful to Allah. He taught his son never to associate partners with Allah, to honour his parents, that even a mustard seed's deed is seen by Allah, to pray, enjoin good, be patient, not to turn his cheek in pride, to walk humbly and lower his voice.
legacy: Surah Luqman is a short course in faith and manners that parents still teach today.
note: Most scholars say he was a wise man, not a prophet. The commentators describe him as an African, from Nubia or Abyssinia, possibly a former slave; his era is uncertain.

name: The Son of Luqman
line: The son to whom Luqman addressed his famous counsel: O my son, do not associate anything with Allah.
story: Luqman begins each piece of advice with the tender words 'O my dear son'. The son is silent in the Quran, but the whole surah is spoken to him: about Allah's oneness, prayer, patience, humility and a gentle voice. He stands for every child taught by a loving parent.
lesson: The best inheritance a parent leaves is good advice given with love.
note: The Quran does not name him; names such as Tharan or An'am come from the commentators.

name: Bilqis
line: The wise Queen of Saba who consulted her council, tested Sulayman with a gift, and submitted to Allah.
story: The hoopoe found her people worshipping the sun. Sulayman's letter began: in the name of Allah, the Most Merciful. She asked her chiefs' advice and sent a gift rather than war. When she came to Sulayman, her own throne was there before her, and his glass floor looked like water. She said: I submit with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
lesson: Wise leadership listens, weighs, and is willing to change.
when: In the reign of Sulayman (traditional, around 950 BCE)
note: The Quran calls her only 'a woman ruling them'; the name Bilqis comes from the commentators. That Sulayman married her is from Isra'iliyyat.

name: Asif ibn Barkhiya
role: One with knowledge of the Book
line: The man with knowledge of the Book who brought Bilqis's throne before Sulayman in the blink of an eye.
story: After an ifrit offered to fetch the throne before Sulayman stood up, one who had knowledge from the Book said: I will bring it before your glance returns. And there it was. Sulayman did not boast; he said: this is from the favour of my Lord, to test me whether I am grateful or ungrateful.
lesson: Gifts are tests of gratitude, however great they are.
note: The Quran does not name him. Most commentators say he was Asif ibn Barkhiya, Sulayman's scribe or minister; others say Jibril, al-Khidr, or Sulayman himself.

name: Uzayr
role: The man who slept a century
line: A figure revered by some Jews, often identified with the man Allah caused to die for a hundred years.
story: The Quran rebukes those who called Uzayr a son of Allah. Many commentators link him to the man who passed a ruined town and asked: how will Allah give this life after its death? Allah made him die for a hundred years, then raised him. His food had not spoiled, and he watched his donkey's bones be clothed with flesh.
lesson: The One who brings dead bones to life can bring a ruined city back.
when: After the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem (date unknown)
note: Named only in 9:30. Many identify him with Ezra the scribe. That the man of 2:259 was Uzayr is a common view, not stated in the Quran; others say he was Armiya (Jeremiah). Whether he was a prophet is uncertain.

name: Dhul-Qarnayn
line: A righteous king given power on earth, who travelled east and west and built a wall against Yajuj and Majuj.
story: Allah gave him the means to everything. He went to where the sun set into a murky spring, then to where it rose over a people without shelter, judging fairly. Between two mountains he met a people terrorised by Yajuj and Majuj. Refusing payment, he had them bring iron and copper and built a barrier, saying: this is a mercy from my Lord.
lesson: Power used with justice and humility is credited to Allah, not to oneself.
when: Unknown; often placed in the 6th century BCE (if Cyrus)
note: His identity is debated. Many modern scholars favour Cyrus the Great; older writers often said Alexander, which Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn Kathir rejected since Alexander was a pagan; others suggest a Himyarite king. Whether he was a prophet is also disputed; most say a righteous king.

name: Imran
line: Maryam's father, whose family Allah chose above the worlds, and after whom Surah Al Imran is named.
story: Allah chose Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran over the worlds. Imran was a righteous man of Bani Israil. Maryam is called 'daughter of Imran' in the Quran, and through her came Isa. The commentators say Imran died before Maryam was born.
legacy: The third surah of the Quran bears his family's name.
note: Not the same as Imran (Amram) the father of Musa and Harun, although some have confused the two.

name: Hannah
line: The wife of Imran, who dedicated her unborn child to Allah's service and named her Maryam.
story: While pregnant she prayed: my Lord, I have vowed what is in my womb to You, freed for Your service, so accept it from me. When a girl was born she said: the male is not like the female. She named her Maryam and asked Allah to protect her and her children from Shaytan. Allah accepted her with a goodly acceptance.
legacy: The Prophet ﷺ said Shaytan did not touch Maryam and her son at birth, which Abu Hurayrah linked to her prayer (3:36).
lesson: A mother's sincere intention before her child is born can shape a whole story.
note: The Quran calls her 'the wife of Imran'; the name Hannah (Hanna bint Faqudh) comes from the commentators.

name: The Wife of Zakariya
line: Zakariya's wife, barren for years, whom Allah made fit to bear Yahya in old age.
story: Zakariya prayed for an heir, though he was old and his wife barren. Allah answered and gave him Yahya, and 'amended his wife for him'. The Quran praises the household together: they hastened to good deeds, called on Allah in hope and fear, and were humble before Him.
lesson: Nothing is too late for Allah to give.
when: Shortly before the birth of Isa
note: The Quran does not name her. The commentators call her Ishba or Elisabeth and say she was a relative of Maryam's mother.

name: The Disciples of Isa
line: The close followers of Isa who answered his call: we are the helpers of Allah.
story: When Isa sensed disbelief from his people, he asked: who are my helpers for Allah? The disciples replied: we are the helpers of Allah, we believe, bear witness that we are Muslims. They asked for a table spread with food from heaven, so that their hearts might be at rest. The Quran tells believers to be helpers of Allah as they were.
lesson: Answering the call to help the truth is what made them honoured.
note: The Quran does not give their number or names; the twelve names are from Christian sources.

name: The Messengers of the Town
line: Two messengers sent to a town and a third sent to strengthen them, all rejected by its people.
story: Allah sent two messengers to a town; when the people called them liars, He reinforced them with a third. The people said: you are only men like us, and we see you as a bad omen. The messengers answered: your omen is with yourselves. Then a man came running from the far end of the town to support them.
lesson: Messengers ask no payment; their only duty is to deliver clearly.
when: Unknown; some commentators place it after Isa
note: Many commentators say the town was Antioch and the messengers were sent by Isa. Ibn Kathir argued they were messengers of Allah from an earlier time, since Antioch was the first city to accept Isa's message.

name: Habib al-Najjar
line: The man who ran from the far end of the city to defend the messengers, and was told: enter Paradise.
story: He came running: O my people, follow the messengers, those who ask no payment and are rightly guided. Why should I not worship the One who created me? His people killed him. He was told: enter Paradise. Even then he thought of them: if only my people knew how my Lord has forgiven me.
lesson: He wished good for his people even after they killed him.
when: Unknown; some commentators place it after Isa
note: The Quran calls him only 'a man'; the name Habib al-Najjar (the carpenter) comes from the commentators. A mosque in Antakya bears his name.

name: The People of the Cave
line: Young believers who fled a pagan ruler into a cave, and Allah made them sleep for 309 years.
story: They were youths who believed in their Lord, and Allah increased them in guidance. Refusing their people's idols, they took refuge in a cave with their dog. Allah made them sleep three hundred years and nine more, turning them in their sleep. When they woke, one went to town with an old silver coin, and their secret was discovered.
legacy: Their story in Surah al-Kahf is read by Muslims every Friday.
lesson: Allah protects those who flee to Him to protect their faith.
when: Commonly placed around 250 CE, under Roman persecution (traditional)
note: The Quran says only Allah knows their number (18:22). Ephesus is the oldest claim; a cave near Amman, Jordan, and others are also proposed. The ruler's name Decius and their names come from Christian and later sources.

name: The Owner of the Two Gardens
line: A rich man in a Quranic parable who boasted his gardens would never perish, until they did.
story: Allah gave him two gardens of grapevines, ringed with palms, a river between them. He told his poorer companion: I have more wealth and men than you, and I do not think this will ever end. The companion warned him: why did you not say, what Allah wills? By morning his gardens were ruined, and he wrung his hands: if only I had not associated anyone with my Lord.
lesson: Say 'ma sha Allah' over your blessings; everything you own is on loan.
note: The Quran presents it as a parable. Some commentators say it describes two real brothers, possibly of Bani Israil.

name: The Companions of the Garden
line: Brothers who swore to harvest their orchard at dawn so no poor person could share it, and lost it overnight.
story: They vowed to pick their fruit early in the morning and said no 'if Allah wills'. In the night a calamity swept the garden, leaving it like a harvested field. They set out whispering: let no poor person come in on you today. Seeing it ruined, they thought they were lost. The most moderate of them reminded them, and they repented.
lesson: Wealth withheld from the poor can vanish overnight.
note: The commentators say the garden was at Darawan near Sana'a and that their father used to give the poor their share; these details are not in the Quran.

name: Tubba
line: A king of Yemen whose people were destroyed, though the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have forbidden cursing Tubba himself.
story: The Quran twice names 'the people of Tubba' among the nations destroyed for denying their messengers. Tubba was the title of the kings of Himyar. Many commentators say this Tubba, often named As'ad Abu Karib, came to Madinah, turned to the faith of the rabbis there, and honoured the Kaaba by covering it.
lesson: A ruler can believe while his people do not, and each will answer for himself.
note: Which Tubba is meant is debated. The narration 'Do not curse Tubba, for he had become Muslim' is reported by Ahmad and others, and its chain is discussed. Reports that he first covered the Kaaba come from the historians.

name: The Woman Who Undid Her Yarn
line: A woman in a Quranic image who spun strong thread, then unravelled it: a picture of breaking promises.
story: Allah warns: do not be like her who undid her spun thread after it was strong, by using your oaths to deceive one another. The commentators say there was such a woman in Makkah who spun all day and undid it in the evening. The image fits anyone who builds trust and then throws it away.
lesson: A broken promise unravels everything good you built before it.
when: Makkah, before or during the Prophet's time ﷺ
note: The commentators name her Rayta bint Sa'd of Quraysh; others say the verse is only a parable.

name: Zayd ibn Haritha
line: The Prophet's beloved freedman and adopted son, the only Companion named in the Quran.
story: Taken as a slave as a boy, he was given to the Prophet ﷺ, who freed him. When his family came to buy him back, Zayd chose to stay. He was called Zayd ibn Muhammad until verse 33:5 ended adoption by name. The Quran names him in 33:37 over his marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh. He fell as commander at Mu'tah.
legacy: His son Usamah led an army as a young man, showing how far a freedman's family could rise in Islam.
when: About 581 to 629 CE; died at Mu'tah, 8 AH
note: Among the very first to accept Islam. His birth year is approximate.

name: Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum
line: The blind Companion whose visit opens Surah Abasa, and whom the Prophet ﷺ honoured ever after.
story: He came asking to learn while the Prophet ﷺ was busy calling the leaders of Quraysh. The Prophet ﷺ frowned and turned to them, and Allah revealed: he frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him. Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ greeted him warmly, made him a muezzin with Bilal, and left him in charge of Madinah when he travelled.
lesson: A sincere seeker counts for more with Allah than a powerful man who does not care.
when: Makkah and Madinah; said to have died at al-Qadisiyyah, 636 CE
note: That Abasa was revealed about him is reported by al-Tirmidhi from Aishah. That 'except those with a disability' in 4:95 was added on his request is reported by al-Bukhari. His death at Qadisiyyah is the common report; some say he died in Madinah.

name: Khawlah bint Tha'labah
line: The woman whose complaint about her husband Allah heard from above the seven heavens.
story: Her husband Aws ibn al-Samit declared her 'like his mother's back', an old Arab way of ending a marriage. She came to the Prophet ﷺ and argued for herself and her children, complaining to Allah. Aishah, in the same room, could not hear all she said, yet Allah revealed: Allah has heard the words of the one who disputes with you about her husband.
legacy: Her case ended the pre-Islamic practice of zihar and set the rules of expiation.
lesson: No complaint made sincerely to Allah goes unheard.
note: Her name is also given as Khuwaylah bint Malik ibn Tha'labah. The story is reported by Abu Dawud and others; Aishah's remark is cited by al-Bukhari.

name: The Three Who Stayed Behind
line: Three believers who stayed home from Tabuk without excuse, told the truth, and were forgiven after fifty days.
story: Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabi and Hilal ibn Umayyah did not go to Tabuk, and unlike the hypocrites they refused to make excuses. The Prophet ﷺ told the Muslims not to speak to them. For fifty days the earth felt narrow despite its vastness. Then Allah revealed their forgiveness, and Ka'b said his honesty had saved him.
lesson: Truthfulness, even when it costs you, is the way out.
when: After the Tabuk expedition, 9 AH (630 CE)
note: The Quran does not name them; their names come from Ka'b ibn Malik's own account in al-Bukhari and Muslim.
aliases: The Three Who Were Left Behind
